interpretation.interpretation: The diagram shows the phases of the Moon during one lunar month in relation to the Sun. The Sun (labelled "SOL") is the disc at the right, with radiating strokes. The Moon is drawn at eight positions on a circle around the centre, each with a different shape and a Greek-derived name for the phase, together with its age in days. At "LUNA PRIMA" the Moon is a thin crescent ("MONOIDES") close to the Sun. At day 8 it is a half-disc ("DIATOMOS"). At day 12 it is a larger segment ("AMPHICIRTOS", i.e. gibbous). At day 15 it is a full disc ("PANSELENOS"), at the point farthest from the Sun and joined to the Sun by a straight line. After that the phases reverse: day 18 is gibbous ("AMPHICIRTOS"), day 22 is a half-disc ("DIATOMOS"), and day 27 is a crescent ("MONOIDES"). The two texts in the middle explain the geometry. The upper hemisphere ("EMISPERIU SUPERIUS") is the part "per quod luna recedit a sole", through which the Moon moves away from the Sun, during waxing. The lower hemisphere ("EMISPERIU INFERIUS") is the part "per quod luna propinquat soli", through which the Moon approaches the Sun, during waning. The diagram therefore illustrates the waxing and waning of the Moon as a function of its angular distance from the Sun. The expansion of the abbreviated "p quod" as "per quod" is my reading. The second line is partly obscured by a smudge, and the missing word is read as "luna".
interpretation.evidence: The transcribed labels give the lunar ages ("LUNA ·VIII·", "·XII·", "·XU·", "·XVIII·", "·XXII·", "·XXVII·", "PRIMA") and the phase names ("MONOIDES", "DIATOMOS", "AMPHICIRTOS", "PANSELENOS"). The central texts speak of the Moon receding from and approaching the Sun. The shapes visible in Step 1 agree with the text: crescents, half-discs, segments larger than a half, and a full disc. The Sun disc is marked by radiating strokes, and the straight line joins it to the full-Moon disc. Step 1 problems: entry 1 is flagged in entry 2 as doubtful and should be disregarded. Entry 3 uses "above" although the same two elements are joined in entry 4. The Step 1 reading "XV" for "·XU·" is an interpretation of the written "XU". Several "LUNA" captions were related by loose predicates ("above" or "below") to elements other than the disc they belong to, for example entries 7, 11, 13, 19, 22 and 25, so these low-certainty relations should not be read as meaningful. The relation in entry 12 ("contains") is also loose. In entry 9 the letters on the upper right crescent, "MO NO ID ES", are treated as one label. The Step 1 entry for the lower right crescent reads "MONO" on the crescent and "IDES" along its outer edge. The later "IDES" and "MONOIDES" are the same word. In Step 1, the lower-left "AM phi CIR TOS" was recorded as "CIR TOS" to the left, whereas it is partly written upside down along the curve. The lunar-age number for the top half-disc is "VIII" and for the lower one "XXII"; both are called "DIATOMOS".

interpretation.diagram_classification: computistic / didactic scheme within the tradition of medieval natural science
interpretation.interpretation: The diagram belongs to the tradition of medieval treatises on astronomy and time-reckoning (computus), in which the Latin West transmitted, through Latin intermediaries, Greek terms for the phases of the Moon. It is a teaching figure, with the Sun and the Moon arranged on a circle so that the phases can be read as a sequence through the month. It is not a realistic map of the heavens. The Moon's orbit is a single circle around a central point. The Sun is placed on the circle at one side, and the opposition of Sun and full Moon is shown by the straight line across the middle. The two central texts divide the month into a period of increasing distance from the Sun and a period of return towards it.
interpretation.evidence: The format (a circle, discs of different shapes, labels with numerals, and explanatory text in the middle) is that of a schematic teaching figure. The Latinised Greek terms and the numbering of lunar days are typical of computistic and cosmological texts, but I do not name a specific source because I am not certain of it. The straight line linking the full-Moon disc and the Sun disc is a visual feature recorded in Step 1, entry 15.
